ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> After providing informed consent, participants completed an AM retrieval task.

> All memories were required to have occurred within the past five years and to include events in which participants were personally involved.

> For each memory, participants provided a unique title and an event date.

> When the exact day was unknown, participants were instructed to estimate the date by indicating the beginning (day 1), middle (day 15), or end (day 28) of the month.

> Before providing these ratings, participants were given definitions of both perspectives, explaining that own-eyes memories are experienced from the original viewpoint of the self, whereas observer memories involve viewing the event from an external vantage point in which the self can be seen.

> Participants were informed that memories could be experienced exclusively from one perspective or fluctuate between perspectives.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .087", "ps > .33", "p = .269", "p = .49", "p = .41", "ps > .35"), Sentence = c("In the observer model, the within-person rehearsal coefficient was not significant at the reference memory age (β = -0.034, p = .087), but its interaction with log memory age was negative and significant (β = -0.012, p = .035), indicating that the association between rehearsal and observer ratings became more negative as memory age increased.", "Between-person differences in reliving, rehearsal, and emotional intensity were not significantly associated with either perspective (all ps > .33; see Table S8 for full statistics).", "The interaction was not significant (β = 0.011, SE = 0.010, t(34,813) = 1.11, p = .269).", "Model diagnostics confirmed an adequate basis dimension for the smooth term in both perspectives, with non-significant k-index tests (Observer: k-index = 1.01, p = .49; Own-Eyes: k-index = 1.00, p = .41).", "Model diagnostics confirmed an adequate basis dimension for the smooth term in both perspectives, with non-significant k-index tests (Observer: k-index = 1.01, p = .49; Own-Eyes: k-index = 1.00, p = .41).", "All differences were non-significant (all ps > .35) and all 95% CIs for d included zero." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: After providing informed consent, participants completed an AM retrieval task.
All memories were required to have occurred within the past five years and to include events in which participants were personally involved.
For each memory, participants provided a unique title and an event date.
When the exact day was unknown, participants were instructed to estimate the date by indicating the beginning (day 1), middle (day 15), or end (day 28) of the month.

Before providing these ratings, participants were given definitions of both perspectives, explaining that own-eyes memories are experienced from the original viewpoint of the self, whereas observer memories involve viewing the event from an external vantage point in which the self can be seen.
Participants were informed that memories could be experienced exclusively from one perspective or fluctuate between perspectives.

> format_beta <- function(x, digits = 3) {
>   rounded <- round(x, digits)
>   ifelse(rounded == 0 & x != 0,
>          formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2),
>          formatC(rounded, format = "f", digits = digits))
> }
> format_se <- function(x, digits = 3) {
>   rounded <- round(x, digits)
>   ifelse(rounded != 0, formatC(rounded, format = "f", digits = digits),
>          ifelse(x < 1e-6, formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2), "<.001"))
> }
> get_model_rows <- function(model, model_label, predictor_labels, r2_marginal, r2_conditional) {
>   cf <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))
>   r2_marginal    <- unname(r2_marginal)
>   r2_conditional <- unname(r2_conditional)
>   out <- data.frame(
>     Model       = c(model_label, rep("", nrow(cf) - 1)),
>     Predictor   = c("Intercept", predictor_labels),
>     beta        = format_beta(cf$Estimate),
>     SE          = format_se(cf$`Std. Error`),
>     df          = round(cf$df, 0),
>     t           = round(cf$`t value`, 2),
>     p           = ifelse(cf$`Pr(>|t|)` < .001, "<.001",
>                          as.character(round(cf$`Pr(>|t|)`, 3))),
>     R2_marginal    = c(round(r2_marginal, 3), rep(NA, nrow(cf) - 1)),
>     R2_conditional = c(round(r2_conditional, 3), rep(NA, nrow(cf) - 1))
>   )
>   rownames(out) <- NULL
>   out
> }

> format_beta <- function(x, digits = 3) {
>   rounded <- round(x, digits)
>   ifelse(rounded == 0 & x != 0,
>          formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2),
>          formatC(rounded, format = "f", digits = digits))
> }
> format_se <- function(x, digits = 3) {
>   rounded <- round(x, digits)
>   ifelse(rounded != 0, formatC(rounded, format = "f", digits = digits),
>          ifelse(x < 1e-6, formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2), "<.001"))
> }
> get_model_rows <- function(model, model_label, predictor_labels, r2_marginal, r2_conditional) {
>   cf <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))
>   r2_marginal    <- unname(r2_marginal)
>   r2_conditional <- unname(r2_conditional)
>   out <- data.frame(
>     Model       = c(model_label, rep("", nrow(cf) - 1)),
>     Predictor   = c("Intercept", predictor_labels),
>     beta        = format_beta(cf$Estimate),
>     SE          = format_se(cf$`Std. Error`),
>     df          = round(cf$df, 0),
>     t           = round(cf$`t value`, 2),
>     p           = ifelse(cf$`Pr(>|t|)` < .001, "<.001",
>                          as.character(round(cf$`Pr(>|t|)`, 3))),
>     R2_marginal    = c(round(r2_marginal, 3), rep(NA, nrow(cf) - 1)),
>     R2_conditional = c(round(r2_conditional, 3), rep(NA, nrow(cf) - 1))
>   )
>   rownames(out) <- NULL
>   out
> }

text.text: Autobiographical memories differ systematically with remoteness, yet little is known about the temporal form of these differences or when they are most pronounced.
One consistent change over time concerns visual perspective-as memories become more remote, owneyes perspectives become less prominent and observer-like perspectives more prominent.

Because visual perspective specifies the vantage point from which a remembered event is mentally seen, these shifts may reflect changes in how visual imagery of past events is reconstructed over time.

We examined the temporal trajectory of visual perspective across 18,229 autobiographical memories from 80 participants, using memory age measured in days to characterize its relationship with own-eyes and observer-like perspectives at a finer temporal resolution than in previous work.
For both perspectives, age-related differences followed a negatively accelerated trajectory.
Observer perspective increased and own-eyes perspective decreased most sharply among relatively recent memories, with progressively smaller differences at greater memory ages.
Approximately half of the total modeled difference occurred within the first four months, although the trajectory continued across several years.
Higher reliving and emotional intensity were associated with attenuated age-related shifts in both perspectives, and rehearsal also moderated their trajectories.
These findings show that visual perspective varies nonlinearly across autobiographical memory age and identify the early months after an event as a particularly dynamic period.

More broadly, the results characterize the temporal organization of autobiographical imagery, linking the viewpoint from which past events are visualized to both their remoteness and the subjective qualities of recollection.
Autobiographical memories (AMs) span remarkably long timescales, from events that occurred only hours ago to those remembered years later.
Across these timescales, memories are not static, but can change in both their content and how they are experienced.

More remote AMs tend to contain less episodic detail and are experienced with less vividness and emotional intensity [1] [2] [3] [4] , patterns that may partly reflect reduced accessibility or transformation of event-specific information over time 5, 6.
text.formatted: More remote AMs tend to contain less episodic detail and are experienced with less vividness and emotional intensity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> , patterns that may partly reflect reduced accessibility or transformation of event-specific information over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref>.

text.text: Yet considerably less is known about the temporal form of these differences in memories over time.

Do characteristics of autobiographical remembering vary at a relatively constant rate across memory age, or are the largest differences concentrated relatively early after an event, followed by progressively smaller differences as memories become more remote?

Characterizing this temporal trajectory is important for understanding when autobiographical remembering differs most strongly with remoteness and for identifying the retention intervals over which processes contributing to these differences are most likely to operate.
Visual perspective plays a generative role in autobiographical imagery by shaping how a remembered event is constructed and where the self is located within the imagined scene 7, 8 .
text.formatted: Visual perspective plays a generative role in autobiographical imagery by shaping how a remembered event is constructed and where the self is located within the imagined scene <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Memories can be experienced from an own-eyes perspective, corresponding to the viewpoint from which memories are typically experienced from, and from an observer-like perspective, in which the rememberer could see themself from an external vantage point 9 .
text.formatted: Memories can be experienced from an own-eyes perspective, corresponding to the viewpoint from which memories are typically experienced from, and from an observer-like perspective, in which the rememberer could see themself from an external vantage point <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Own-eyes memories are generally associated with greater sensory detail, reliving, and emotional intensity than observer-like memories [9] [10] [11] , as well as richer reconstruction of scene-based information 12 .
text.formatted: Own-eyes memories are generally associated with greater sensory detail, reliving, and emotional intensity than observer-like memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> , as well as richer reconstruction of scene-based information <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, visual perspective is not simply a passive correlate of memory quality.

Experimentally altering the perspective adopted during retrieval can change the phenomenological experience and remembered content of an event and influence how that event is subsequently remembered [13] [14] [15] .
text.formatted: Experimentally altering the perspective adopted during retrieval can change the phenomenological experience and remembered content of an event and influence how that event is subsequently remembered <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> .

text.text: Visual perspective therefore provides a window onto the constructive organization of autobiographical remembering.
Visual perspective also varies reliably with memory remoteness.

Retrospective studies consistently show that relatively recent memories are more strongly associated with an own-eyes perspective, whereas more remote memories are increasingly associated with an observer-like perspective 3, 9, 11, 12 .
text.formatted: Retrospective studies consistently show that relatively recent memories are more strongly associated with an own-eyes perspective, whereas more remote memories are increasingly associated with an observer-like perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Prospective studies further demonstrate that perspective can change within individual memories across repeated retrievals 4, 16 , although such changes can occur in both directions.
text.formatted: Prospective studies further demonstrate that perspective can change within individual memories across repeated retrievals <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> , although such changes can occur in both directions.

text.text: What remains unclear is the functional form of the relationship between visual perspective and memory age.

Previous studies have typically compared broad temporal categories or followed relatively small numbers of memories across a limited number of retrieval occasions, making it difficult to determine whether age-related differences accumulate uniformly or are disproportionately concentrated at shorter retention intervals.
Several findings suggest the latter possibility.
Talarico and Rubin 4 observed changes across logarithmically spaced intervals of 7, 42, and 224 days, while Wardell et al. 16 detected perspective shifts across approximately 10 weeks.
text.formatted: Talarico and Rubin <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> observed changes across logarithmically spaced intervals of 7, 42, and 224 days, while Wardell et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> detected perspective shifts across approximately 10 weeks.

text.text: Reliable differences across these comparatively short timescales raise the possibility that the relationship between visual perspective and memory age is negatively accelerated, with the greatest differences occurring among relatively recent memories and progressively smaller differences at greater memory ages.
Such a trajectory would parallel a broader property of memory retention.

The temporal distribution and retention of autobiographical information are often characterized by negatively accelerated functions in which change is greatest over shorter intervals and slows with increasing time 5, [17] [18] [19] [20] .
text.formatted: The temporal distribution and retention of autobiographical information are often characterized by negatively accelerated functions in which change is greatest over shorter intervals and slows with increasing time <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref> .

text.text: Although this literature has primarily concerned the accessibility, frequency, or retention of autobiographical information, a comparable temporal form in visual perspective would suggest that the phenomenological organization of remembering also varies most strongly over relatively short retention intervals.

Perspective may be particularly informative in this respect because maintaining an own-eyes viewpoint may depend on access to perceptual and spatial information specifying the original organization of the event, whereas reconstruction from an observer-like viewpoint does not preserve the originally experienced vantage point.

Determining whether visual perspective follows a similar negatively accelerated relationship with memory age can therefore help establish whether this aspect of autobiographical reconstruction varies over a timescale comparable to other forms of memory change.
The strength of the relationship between memory age and visual perspective may also depend on characteristics of the remembered event.

Reliving and emotional intensity are closely associated with visual perspective, with memories experienced with stronger reliving and emotion more likely to be remembered from an own-eyes perspective [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: Reliving and emotional intensity are closely associated with visual perspective, with memories experienced with stronger reliving and emotion more likely to be remembered from an own-eyes perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref> .

text.text: Some evidence also suggests that these characteristics may be more stable for phenomenologically stronger memories.

For example, Talarico and Rubin 4 , found that flashbulb memories remained relatively stable in perspective across retention intervals, whereas everyday memories from a similar period were more likely to shift toward an observer-like perspective.
text.formatted: For example, Talarico and Rubin <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , found that flashbulb memories remained relatively stable in perspective across retention intervals, whereas everyday memories from a similar period were more likely to shift toward an observer-like perspective.

text.text: Rehearsal may likewise be relevant because repeated retrieval can influence the perspective and episodic information available during subsequent remembering 13 .
text.formatted: Rehearsal may likewise be relevant because repeated retrieval can influence the perspective and episodic information available during subsequent remembering <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: Thus, the temporal relationship between memory age and visual perspective may vary according to the extent to which a memory continues to be strongly relived, emotionally intense, or repeatedly retrieved.
The current study examined the relationship between memory age and visual perspective using a large retrospective dataset of AMs spanning the preceding five years 15, 24 .
text.formatted: The current study examined the relationship between memory age and visual perspective using a large retrospective dataset of AMs spanning the preceding five years <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> .

text.text: Eighty participants generated more than 18,000 memories-over 200 per participant-and provided dates and separate ratings of own-eyes and observer perspective, yielding dense and continuous sampling across memory age.
Our primary aim was to determine the functional form of the relationship between memory age and visual perspective.
We compared linear and nonlinear models and used generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) 25 to characterize flexibly when age-related differences were most pronounced across the retention interval.
text.formatted: We compared linear and nonlinear models and used generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25</ref> to characterize flexibly when age-related differences were most pronounced across the retention interval.

text.text: We predicted a negatively accelerated trajectory, such that observer perspective would increase and own-eyes perspective would decrease most sharply among relatively recent memories, with progressively smaller differences at greater memory ages.

As a secondary aim, we examined whether reliving, emotional intensity, and rehearsal moderated these relationships, testing whether the temporal trajectory varied as a function of the phenomenological strength and retrieval history of the remembered event.

The two datasets did not differ significantly in memory age or any of the measured memory characteristics, and the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar across studies (Supplementary Tables S2-S3 and Figure S1-S2).
text.formatted: The two datasets did not differ significantly in memory age or any of the measured memory characteristics, and the pattern of intercorrelations was highly similar across studies (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2-S3</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1-S2</ref>).

text.text: We therefore combined the datasets for subsequent analyses.
We first examined whether visual perspective varied as a function of memory age.
For each perspective rating, we compared linear, logarithmic, and quadratic specifications of memory age (see Supplementary Figure S3).
text.formatted: For each perspective rating, we compared linear, logarithmic, and quadratic specifications of memory age (see Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: Memory age significantly predicted both observer and own-eyes perspective ratings across all three models.

For observer ratings, perspective increased with memory age in the linear model (β = 0.055, SE = .007, t(81) = 8.78), logarithmic model (β = 0.166, SE = 0.019, t(79) = 8.54), and quadratic model (β = 32.84, SE = 3.75, t(80) = 8.76).

Conversely, own-eyes ratings decreased with memory age in the linear model (β = -0.06, SE = 0.006, t(77) = -10.5), logarithmic model (β = -0.181, SE = 0.018, t(79) = -9.98), and quadratic model (β = -35.68, SE = 3.43, t(77) = -10.41).

Model comparisons indicated that the logarithmic model provided the best fit for both perspectives (see Table 1 and Tables S4-S5), with lower AIC values than either the linear model (observer: ΔAIC = 97.54; own-eyes: ΔAIC = 119.68) or the quadratic model (observer: ΔAIC = 66.64; own-eyes: ΔAIC = 80.09).
text.formatted: Model comparisons indicated that the logarithmic model provided the best fit for both perspectives (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and Tables <ref type="table">S4-S5</ref>), with lower AIC values than either the linear model (observer: ΔAIC = 97.54; own-eyes: ΔAIC = 119.68) or the quadratic model (observer: ΔAIC = 66.64; own-eyes: ΔAIC = 80.09).

text.text: As shown in Figure 1, observer ratings increased with memory age whereas own-eyes ratings decreased, with both trajectories showing a steeper change at shorter memory ages followed by a progressively shallower rate of change as memories became more remote.
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, observer ratings increased with memory age whereas own-eyes ratings decreased, with both trajectories showing a steeper change at shorter memory ages followed by a progressively shallower rate of change as memories became more remote.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with a negatively accelerated relationship between memory age and visual perspective.

Despite these systematic associations with memory age, the variance explained by the fixed effects was modest.
For observer ratings, marginal R² was .020, compared with a conditional R² of .355 when participant-level random effects were included.
A similar pattern emerged for own-eyes ratings, with a marginal R² of .026 and a conditional R² of .375.

Thus, although memory age was systematically associated with shifts in perspective, substantial variability was attributable to individual differences in the overall tendency to remember events from particular perspectives.
The power function model showed that the power exponent was significant for both observer (b = 0.062, SE = 0.007, p < .001) and own-eyes ratings (b = -0.044, SE = 0.005, p < .001).
text.formatted: The power function model showed that the power exponent was significant for both observer (b = 0.062, SE = 0.007, p < .001) and own-eyes ratings (b = -0.044, SE = 0.005, p < .001).

text.text: In both cases, the estimated exponents were consistent with a negatively accelerated trajectory in which the rate of change diminished with increasing memory age.
The marginal R² for the power model was .020 for observer and .021 owneyes ratings, compared with .020 and .026, respectively, for the logarithmic models.

Although these values should not be interpreted as formal model comparisons because of the different outcome scales, the power-function analyses converged with the primary analyses in supporting a nonlinear, decelerating relationship between memory age and visual perspective.
The results were consistent when the two studies were modeled separately (Table S6) and when memories in the earliest time point were excluded (Table S7).
text.formatted: The results were consistent when the two studies were modeled separately (Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>) and when memories in the earliest time point were excluded (Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: In summary, memory age predicted systematic shifts in both perspectives, with observer ratings increasing and own-eyes ratings decreasing as memories became more remote.

Among the directly comparable models, the logarithmic function provided the best fit, while the power-function analyses provided converging evidence for the broader negatively accelerated trajectory characterized by greater change at shorter memory ages and progressively slower change over time.

In the own-eyes model, rehearsal predicted higher own-eyes ratings (β = 0.130, p < .001) and a significant interaction with memory age (β = 0.016, p = .003).

text.text: In the observer model, the within-person rehearsal coefficient was not significant at the reference memory age (β = -0.034, p = .087), but its interaction with log memory age was negative and significant (β = -0.012, p = .035), indicating that the association between rehearsal and observer ratings became more negative as memory age increased.
Between-person differences in reliving, rehearsal, and emotional intensity were not significantly associated with either perspective (all ps > .33; see Table S8 for full statistics).
text.formatted: Between-person differences in reliving, rehearsal, and emotional intensity were not significantly associated with either perspective (all ps > .33; see Table <ref type="table">S8</ref> for full statistics).

text.text: The preceding model comparisons indicated that changes in visual perspective were better characterized by a negatively accelerated than a linear trajectory.

To characterize the timing of these changes more flexibly, we next fit GAMMs, which allowed the relationship between memory age and perspective to vary nonlinearly without imposing a specific functional form.
The GAMMs indicated significant nonlinear associations between memory age and both perspective ratings.
Observer ratings increased most rapidly among relatively recent memories, followed by a progressively slower rate of increase as memories became more remote (edf = 3.46, F = 662.7, p < .001).
text.formatted: Observer ratings increased most rapidly among relatively recent memories, followed by a progressively slower rate of increase as memories became more remote (edf = 3.46, F = 662.7, p < .001).

text.text: Own-eyes ratings showed the complementary pattern, decreasing most rapidly among relatively recent memories and more gradually for more remote memories (edf = 4.47, F = 940.4, p < .001).
text.formatted: Own-eyes ratings showed the complementary pattern, decreasing most rapidly among relatively recent memories and more gradually for more remote memories (edf = 4.47, F = 940.4, p < .001).

text.text: To characterize the time course of perspective change, we used the log-scale GAMM to estimate when each perspective reached 25%, 50%, 75%, and 90% of its total modeled change.
Both perspectives changed most rapidly at the earliest observed memory age, with the rate of change gradually slowing thereafter.
This pattern was consistent with a logarithmic trajectory without an interior peak (Table 2 and Figure 3; the same milestones are shown on the raw rating scale in Figure S4).
text.formatted: This pattern was consistent with a logarithmic trajectory without an interior peak (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>; the same milestones are shown on the raw rating scale in Figure <ref type="figure">S4</ref>).

text.text: The timing of the milestones differed somewhat by perspective.
Own-eyes reached 25% of its total change sooner than observer (approximately 5 vs. 10 days), while the two perspectives reached 50% at nearly the same time (117 vs. 118 days).
At the later milestones, observer reached each sooner than own-eyes: 75% at approximately 584 vs. 650 days (19.2 vs.
21.4 months) and 90% at 1,164 vs. 1,213 days (38.3 vs.
39.9 months).
The estimated rate of change at the earliest observed memory age was also much higher than at 30 days: approximately 51 times higher for observer and 97 times higher for own-eyes.
Although the milestone analysis suggested small timing differences between the two perspectives, it did not directly test whether their rates of change differed.

To compare rates directly, own-eyes ratings were reversed onto the same scale direction as observer ratings (8own-eyes), and a linear mixed model was fit with perspective, log(memory age), and their interaction.
The interaction was not significant (β = 0.011, SE = 0.010, t(34,813) = 1.11, p = .269).

The estimated slopes were similar for observer (β = 0.165, SE = 0.007) and reversed own-eyes (β = 0.176, SE = 0.007), providing no evidence that their linear rates of change over log memory age differed.
A supplementary GAMM analysis allowing the rate of change for each perspective to vary across memory age produced the same conclusion (Supplementary Methods).

The simultaneous 95% confidence band for the difference between the perspective-specific derivatives included zero across the entire interval, providing no evidence that observer and own-eyes perspectives differed in their rate of change (Figure S5).
text.formatted: The simultaneous 95% confidence band for the difference between the perspective-specific derivatives included zero across the entire interval, providing no evidence that observer and own-eyes perspectives differed in their rate of change (Figure <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: The present findings provide new insight into how visual perspective changes as AMs become more remote.
Consistent with previous research, observer-like perspectives increased and own-eyes perspectives decreased as memories became more remote 4, 9, 16 .
text.formatted: Consistent with previous research, observer-like perspectives increased and own-eyes perspectives decreased as memories became more remote <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> .

text.text: Critically, these shifts in perspective did not occur at a constant rate.
Both perspectives followed a rapid early change followed by progressively slower change.

Additional analyses characterizing the temporal trajectory further indicated that changes in perspective were concentrated among the most recent memories, and then gradually slowed without fully leveling off within the five-year range.
Finally, the relationship between memory age and visual perspective varied with other characteristics of the memory.
Higher reliving and emotional intensity attenuated the shift in both perspective over time.

Rehearsal also moderated the relationship between shifts in perspective and memory age for own-eyes perspectives, such that the decline in own-eyes ratings with increasing memory age was less pronounced for more frequently rehearsed memories.

Overall, these findings show that visual perspective changes systematically as memories become more remote, while revealing that the trajectory of this change is dynamic: it is most pronounced early in a memory's lifespan and varies with the phenomenological qualities and rehearsal history of the remembered event.
Prior research has established that visual perspective varies with memory remoteness, but has generally not been designed to characterize the functional form of this relationship.

Using dense sampling of AMs within participants, we show that changes in visual perspective follow a negatively accelerated trajectory, with the greatest differences among relatively recent memories and progressively smaller changes as memories become more remote.

Among directly comparable candidate models, the logarithmic function provided the best fit, while a power-function analysis showed a similar pattern of rapid early change followed by progressively slower change.

This convergence is theoretically informative because a similar temporal pattern characterizes forgetting, with the greatest loss of memory information occurring over shorter retention intervals and progressively smaller losses thereafter 20, 26 .
text.formatted: This convergence is theoretically informative because a similar temporal pattern characterizes forgetting, with the greatest loss of memory information occurring over shorter retention intervals and progressively smaller losses thereafter <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> .

text.text: One possibility, therefore, is that perspective shifts are related to declining availability of event-specific information that supports the reconstruction of an event from its original vantage point.

As perceptual and spatial information from the original experience becomes less accessible, remembering the event from an own-eyes perspective may become more difficult, increasing the likelihood that it is reconstructed from an observerlike viewpoint.
In this sense, the shift toward observer perspective may be one phenomenological manifestation of broader transformations in how autobiographical events are represented as they become more remote.
A broader possibility is that changes in visual perspective reflect transformations in AM representations as they become more remote.
According to memory transformation accounts, richly detailed episodic representations may become increasingly more like schematic or generalized representations over time 6 .
text.formatted: According to memory transformation accounts, richly detailed episodic representations may become increasingly more like schematic or generalized representations over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: From this perspective, own-eyes remembering may be more readily supported when the original perceptual and spatial organization of an event can be reinstated, whereas observerlike remembering may become more likely as reconstruction depends less strongly on the original viewpoint.
Interestingly, neuroimaging evidence also indicates that the neural representations supporting AM continue to change substantially over this period.

Barry et al. 27 , for example, found that memory specific representations in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex changed nonmonotonically with memory age, increasing towards a peak at approximately 8-12 months before declining and later re-emerging for more remote memories.
text.formatted: Barry et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27</ref> , for example, found that memory specific representations in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex changed nonmonotonically with memory age, increasing towards a peak at approximately 8-12 months before declining and later re-emerging for more remote memories.

text.text: Although these neural changes cannot be directly equated with the changes in visual perspective, they demonstrate that AM representations undergo substantial and protracted reorganization as memories age.

The present behavioral trajectory showed a similarly extended time course: roughly half of the predicted perspective shift had occurred within the first few months, but change continued thereafter and did not approach its slowest phase until several years later.
Thus, rather than marking a discrete transition from recent to remote memory, visual perspective may change alongside the broader, gradual transformation of AM representations over time.
Visual perspective may therefore provide a phenomenological indicator of changes in how AMs are represented with increasing remoteness.
By characterizing the temporal trajectory our findings also provide new insight into when shifts in visual perspective are most likely to occur.
The greatest estimated rates of change were observed among the most recent memories, followed by progressively smaller changes as memories became more remote.
This temporal pattern helps place previous findings in context.
Prospective studies examining memories across relatively short retention intervals (e.g., 16 ), may disproportionately capture the period during which perspective is changing most rapidly.
text.formatted: Prospective studies examining memories across relatively short retention intervals (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> ), may disproportionately capture the period during which perspective is changing most rapidly.

text.text: Indeed, the estimated rate of change declined sharply within the first month, suggesting that studies beginning even a month or two after an event may miss much of this early change.

Conversely, retrospective studies comparing memories across much broader intervals (e.g., 11, 28 ) may reflect differences that emerged disproportionately during the earlier months rather than change accumulating uniformly across the entire retention interval.
text.formatted: Conversely, retrospective studies comparing memories across much broader intervals (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28</ref> ) may reflect differences that emerged disproportionately during the earlier months rather than change accumulating uniformly across the entire retention interval.

text.text: The present findings therefore help narrow the temporal window in which future longitudinal studies could most directly examine the processes that predict whether an AM maintains its original perspective or shifts toward an observer-like viewpoint.
The relationship between memory age and visual perspective also varied with the phenomenological qualities of the memory.

Higher reliving and emotional intensity attenuated the relationship between memory age and both perspectives: the positive association between memory age and observer perspective and the negative association between memory age and own-eyes perspective were both weaker for memories rated higher on these qualities.

This pattern is consistent with Talarico and Rubin 4 , who found that visual perspective remained relatively stable for flashbulb memories while everyday memories showed a greater shift toward an observer perspective over time.
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with Talarico and Rubin <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , who found that visual perspective remained relatively stable for flashbulb memories while everyday memories showed a greater shift toward an observer perspective over time.

text.text: If perspective shifts partly reflect reduced access to eventspecific information, memories that retain a stronger sense of reliving and emotional intensity may also retain more of the perceptual and spatial information that supports reconstruct from the original viewpoint.

In this sense, the moderation findings are consistent with the possibility that phenomenologically richer memories are relatively resistant to the changes in perspective that accompany increasing remoteness.
This interpretation is also broadly compatible with accounts in which richly recollected, eventspecific memories continue to rely on hippocampally supported representations 29.
text.formatted: This interpretation is also broadly compatible with accounts in which richly recollected, eventspecific memories continue to rely on hippocampally supported representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">29</ref>.

text.text: Emotional intensity may be related to perspective change through an additional route.
Visual perspective can itself influence the emotional experience of autobiographical remembering, with observer-like perspectives often associated with reduced affect 30.
text.formatted: Visual perspective can itself influence the emotional experience of autobiographical remembering, with observer-like perspectives often associated with reduced affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">30</ref>.

text.text: The weaker perspective shifts observed for more emotionally intense memories may therefore reflect the close coupling between visual perspective and emotional experience, in addition to the persistence of event-specific information.
Although these interaction effects were small, their consistency across both perspective measures suggests that the temporal trajectory of perspective change varies systematically across AMs.
Rehearsal showed a somewhat different pattern.
More frequently rehearsed memories showed a weaker decline in own-eyes perspective with increasing memory age, and own-eyes ratings were also higher overall.
This pattern raises the possibility that repeated retrieval helps maintain access to aspects of an event that support remembering from the original vantage point.
Consistent with this possibility, experimental work shows that the perspective adopted during retrieval can alter the episodic information that remains accessible on subsequent retrievals 13, 31 .
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, experimental work shows that the perspective adopted during retrieval can alter the episodic information that remains accessible on subsequent retrievals <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">31</ref> .

text.text: Repeatedly retrieving a memory from an own-eyes perspective may therefore help preserve information that supports that perspective, although this interpretation requires direct longitudinal testing.

More broadly, the perspective-specific association with rehearsal is compatible with evidence that own-eyes and observer perspectives are dissociable rather than mutually exclusive 11 , suggesting that they may share some retrieval dynamics while remaining differentially sensitive to particular memory characteristics.
text.formatted: More broadly, the perspective-specific association with rehearsal is compatible with evidence that own-eyes and observer perspectives are dissociable rather than mutually exclusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , suggesting that they may share some retrieval dynamics while remaining differentially sensitive to particular memory characteristics.

text.text: The present findings also provide specific guidance for future longitudinal research.

Following the same memories across time will be important for determining whether changes in visual perspective accompany, precede, or follow changes in other features of autobiographical remembering.
The temporal trajectory found here suggests that sampling should be densest during the earliest retention intervals, when perspective change appears to be most pronounced.

Combining such longitudinal designs with neuroimaging would further allow researchers to test whether shifts in visual perspective correspond to changes in the neural systems supporting AM retrieval 8 .
text.formatted: Combining such longitudinal designs with neuroimaging would further allow researchers to test whether shifts in visual perspective correspond to changes in the neural systems supporting AM retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: This approach could directly test whether visual perspective serves as a phenomenological marker of broader representational transformation in AM over time.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, the retrospective design does not allow direct observation of changes in perspective within the same memories over time.
Differences across memory ages may therefore reflect both within-memory change and differences in which memories are retained or sampled at different retention intervals.
Memory age was also estimated retrospectively and may be subject to dating error 32, 33 .
text.formatted: Memory age was also estimated retrospectively and may be subject to dating error <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">33</ref> .

text.text: Nevertheless, longitudinal research demonstrates that visual perspective can change within individual memories over time 4 .
text.formatted: Nevertheless, longitudinal research demonstrates that visual perspective can change within individual memories over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, such shifts can occur in both directions over relatively short intervals 16 , indicating that the age-related trajectory observed here should not be interpreted as a uniform progression from own-eyes to observer perspective within every memory.
text.formatted: Importantly, such shifts can occur in both directions over relatively short intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> , indicating that the age-related trajectory observed here should not be interpreted as a uniform progression from own-eyes to observer perspective within every memory.

text.text: Second, because all phenomenological characteristics were assessed concurrently with visual perspective at retrieval, the causal direction of their associations with perspective cannot be determined.
These characteristics may influence perspective change, result from changes in perspective, or reflect other properties of the memory.
Third, the present study was restricted to memories from the preceding five years, limiting conclusions about whether similar trajectories extend to more remote AMs.
The present study provides the first characterization of the trajectory of visual perspective change in AMs using dense sampling across continuous memory age.
Visual perspective changed systematically with increasing remoteness, with the most rapid changes occurring shortly after an event and slowing thereafter.
This temporal pattern is broadly consistent with accounts proposing substantial reorganization of memory representations during the earlier stages of memory transformation 6, 27 .
text.formatted: This temporal pattern is broadly consistent with accounts proposing substantial reorganization of memory representations during the earlier stages of memory transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27</ref> .

text.text: The trajectory also varied with the phenomenological qualities of the remembered event, such that memories associated with greater reliving and emotional intensity showed less pronounced perspective change whereas rehearsal slowed the rate of change in both perspectives but altered the overall level only for own-eyes ratings.

More broadly, these findings highlight visual perspective as a potentially valuable behavioral marker of memory transformation, linking changes in the subjective experience of remembering with broader changes in how AMs are represented over time.
The data were drawn from two previously conducted studies that employed identical procedures 15, 24 .
text.formatted: The data were drawn from two previously conducted studies that employed identical procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> .

text.text: The combined sample consisted of 80 (40 from each study) young adults aged between 18 and 30 years. (n = 46 female; Mage = 21.6 years, SD = 3.19), who reported no history of neurological or psychiatric episodes or current use of medication.
The study was conducted in person.
After providing informed consent, participants completed an AM retrieval task.
First, they were provided with a list of possible events (e.g., camping, going on a date) to help generate AMs.
The recalled memories did not need to be personally significant but had to involve a clearly identifiable episode that was experienced at a specific time and place.
All memories were required to have occurred within the past five years and to include events in which participants were personally involved.
Each participant was asked to generate 228 24 or 240 15 memories.
text.formatted: Each participant was asked to generate 228 <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> or 240 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> memories.

text.text: For each memory, participants provided a unique title and an event date.
Participants reported the event date in month/day/year format as accurately as possible.
When the exact day was unknown, participants were instructed to estimate the date by indicating the beginning (day 1), middle (day 15), or end (day 28) of the month.
Additionally, they were asked to rate their subjective experience related to each memory on the following four characteristics (based on 34 ):
text.formatted: Additionally, they were asked to rate their subjective experience related to each memory on the following four characteristics (based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">34</ref> ):

text.text: Visual Perspective.
Participants rated the extent to which they remembered the event from an own-eyes perspective and from an observer perspective, using separate scales (1 = not at all,7 = completely).

Before providing these ratings, participants were given definitions of both perspectives, explaining that own-eyes memories are experienced from the original viewpoint of the self, whereas observer memories involve viewing the event from an external vantage point in which the self can be seen.
Participants were informed that memories could be experienced exclusively from one perspective or fluctuate between perspectives.

Participants rated the extent to which they experienced a sense of reliving the event (1 = not at all,7 = as clearly as if it were happening now), reflecting the subjective feeling of reexperiencing the event again.
Participants rated the intensity of the emotion arousal associated with the memory (1 = none,7 = high), regardless of whether the emotion was positive or negative.
Participants rated how often they had thought or talked about the event since it occurred (1 = not at all,7 = more than any other memory).
There was an additional emotional valence rating in the St.
Jacques et al., 24 study, however, we focused only on ratings common in both studies.
text.formatted: Jacques et al., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> study, however, we focused only on ratings common in both studies.

text.text: It took participants approximately 5 hours to generate the memories and to rate and date them.
Aggregate data from a subset of these memories, shown during a later fMRI session, are reported in St.
Jacques et al. 15 and St.

text.text: Data were analyzed using R 35 within RStudio 36 using linear mixed-effects models to account for the hierarchical structure of memories nested within participants.
Separate models were conducted for observer and own-eyes ratings.
Statistical significance was assessed at α = .05.

ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used to assist with manuscript preparation, including improving the clarity and organization of text, refining scientific language, and discussing the presentation of statistical analyses.
All analytical decisions, scientific interpretations, and final manuscript content were reviewed and approved by the authors, who retain full responsibility for the work.
To characterize the functional form of the relationship between memory age and visual perspective, we fitted separate linear mixed-effects models for observer and own-eyes ratings.
We compared linear, logarithmic, and quadratic specifications of memory age, with participant-level random intercepts and slopes.
Linear and quadratic memory age terms were rescaled by dividing by 100 to facilitate model estimation.
Models were compared using AIC and BIC.
We additionally fitted power functions as a convergent test of a negatively accelerated relationship.

Because these models used log-transformed perspective ratings, their AIC and BIC values were not directly comparable with models fitted to the original rating scale; marginal R² and the estimated exponent were therefore used descriptively.
Intercept-only models confirmed substantial between-person variability for both observer (ICC = .316) and own-eyes (ICC = .336) ratings, justifying the use of multilevel modeling for all analyses.
The best-fitting model was chosen to investigate whether memory qualities moderate the relationship between memory age and perspective.
Prior to modeling each characteristic was decomposed into within-and between-person components.

While the within-person component was calculated as the memory-level deviation from each participant's own mean rating, the between-person component was calculated as each participant's own rating relative to the sample mean.
This approach allows us to distinguish memory to memory fluctuations from individual differences.

Then, to examine whether memory qualities moderated changes in visual perspective over time, separate linear mixed-effects models were fit for observer and own-eyes ratings and for each memory quality (emotional intensity, reliving, and rehearsal).

Those models predict each perspective rating from the within-person component, between-person component, and the interaction between the within-person component and Log(Memory Age), with a random intercept for participants and random slopes for Log(Memory Age) and the within-person component.

To characterize the temporal trajectory without imposing a particular parametric form, we fitted GAMMs 25 predicting each perspective rating from a smooth function of log(memory age), with participantlevel random effects.
text.formatted: To characterize the temporal trajectory without imposing a particular parametric form, we fitted GAMMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25</ref> predicting each perspective rating from a smooth function of log(memory age), with participantlevel random effects.

text.text: Models were restricted to the common memory-age range represented in both datasets (0-1820 days).

Derivatives of the fitted smooths were used to characterize changes in slope across memory age and to estimate when 25%, 50%, 75%, and 90% of the total modeled difference across the five-year interval had been reached.
The GAMMs were fit with selection (select = TRUE) and an increased smoothing penalty (gamma = 1.2) to enforce smooth, non-overfit functions and obtain highly reliable estimates of the rate of change.

Model diagnostics confirmed an adequate basis dimension for the smooth term in both perspectives, with non-significant k-index tests (Observer: k-index = 1.01, p = .49; Own-Eyes: k-index = 1.00, p = .41).

text.text: Prior to the main analyses, we assessed the comparability of the two studies.

We first filtered the data to exclude trials where memory age was missing or exceeded 5 years (132 excluded trials in total), and logtransformed memory age for subsequent modeling (Memory Age variable was adjusted to 0.5 days where the original value was 0 to allow for log transformation).
The final dataset included 18,229 memory trials.
The distribution of memory ages across theoretically meaningful time bins is presented in Supplementary Table S1.
text.formatted: The distribution of memory ages across theoretically meaningful time bins is presented in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: Independent samples t-tests were conducted on the subject-level mean scores for memory age, observer perspective, own-eyes perspective, reliving, emotional intensity and rehearsal to test for significant differences between the two studies.

No significant differences were found between the two study samples on any of the compared variables (memory age, observer, own-eyes perspective, reliving, emotional intensity, rehearsal, see Supplementary Table S2 and Supplementary Figure S1).
text.formatted: No significant differences were found between the two study samples on any of the compared variables (memory age, observer, own-eyes perspective, reliving, emotional intensity, rehearsal, see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> and Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>).

text.text: These results indicate that, at the subject level, the memories sampled from both studies were statistically equivalent in terms of age and memory characteristics.
Correlations among all key variables in the combined dataset were computed.
As expected, own-eyes and observer ratings showed a strong negative correlation (r = -.84).
Reliving and emotional intensity were positively associated with own-eyes and negatively associated with observer.
Notably, the correlation between Rehearsal and Memory Age was negligible (r = -.03; see Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: Notably, the correlation between Rehearsal and Memory Age was negligible (r = -.03; see Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, a Mantel test, which assesses the similarity between correlation matrices between two studies, revealed a very high and significant correlation between the intercorrelations of the memory characteristics (own-eyes, observer, reliving, rehearsal, emotional intensity, memory age) in the two studies (r = .969, p = .001; see Supplementary Figure S2).
text.formatted: Furthermore, a Mantel test, which assesses the similarity between correlation matrices between two studies, revealed a very high and significant correlation between the intercorrelations of the memory characteristics (own-eyes, observer, reliving, rehearsal, emotional intensity, memory age) in the two studies (r = .969, p = .001; see Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: This suggests that the internal structure of the measured memory characteristics is highly similar across the two independent samples.
Therefore, the data from the two studies were combined for subsequent modeling.

To evaluate whether the rate of change in observer and own-eyes (reversed) ratings differed as a function of memory age, we fit a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) allowing each perspective's trajectory to vary independently (via perspective-specific smooth terms) across logtransformed, centered memory age, with a random intercept for participant.

The first derivative (i.e., instantaneous rate of change) of each perspective-specific smooth was extracted at 200 evenly spaced points across the memory-age range, and a simultaneous 95% confidence interval was constructed for the difference between the two derivative curves at each point.

text.text: Localized Rate-of-Change Difference Between Observer and Own-Eyes Perspectives.

The purple line and shaded band show the GAMM-estimated difference in instantaneous rate of change between perspectives (Observer minus reversed Own-Eyes) and its simultaneous 95% confidence interval, across log-transformed memory age; the dashed line marks zero.
Figure 1.
Log-Transformed Memory Age Predicts Memory Perspective.
Scatter plots display a random 30% subsample of memory trials for visual clarity.
Solid lines represent modelpredicted values from the best-fitting logarithmic mixed-effects model; shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals.
Observer perspective (blue) increases while Own-Eyes perspective (orange) decreases as a logarithmic function of memory age, reflecting rapid early change followed by gradual stabilization.
Figure 2.
Interactions Between Log Memory Age and Within-Person Memory Characteristics on Observer Perspective and Own-Eyes Perspective.

Lines represent model-predicted Observer and Own-Eyes ratings across log-transformed centered memory age, plotted separately for memories rated low (purple; -1 SD within-person), average (green; mean), and high (dark red; +1 SD within-person) in each memory characteristic relative to a participant's own average.
A. Observer × Reliving, B. Observer × Intensity, C. Observer ×
Figure 3.
Cumulative Change in Memory Perspective Over Time.
Lines represent the percentage of each perspective's total model-predicted change, estimated from the log-scale GAMM, reached at each memory age, for Observer (blue) and Own-Eyes (orange) ratings.
Both perspectives show a logarithmic pattern, with most of the total change occurring soon after encoding and the curve flattening gradually thereafter.

Time Course of Memory Perspective Shifts Estimated by GAMM.
Smooth curves represent GAMM-estimated trajectories for Observer (blue) and Own-Eyes (orange) perspective ratings across memory age (days), on the raw rating scale.
Dotted vertical lines mark the memory age at which each perspective reached 50% of its total predicted change (Observer: about 118 days; Own-Eyes: about 117 days).
Dashed vertical lines mark the 90% milestone (Observer: about 1,164 days, 38.3 months; Own-Eyes: about 1,213 days, 39.9 months).
The analysis was restricted to the common memory age range shared by both studies.
